turns.question: I'm starting to think seriously about retiring but I honestly don't know where to begin. What should I be thinking about?
turns.answer:
The first decision is **when you want your pension to begin**.

At age 56 with 21.5 years of service, Section 11-130 reaches an employee who withdraws after age 55 but before age 60 and has at least 10 years of service. For an employee with 20 or more years of service, it provides an age-and-service annuity based on the amounts credited for that annuity, calculated at the employee’s age when withdrawing. [40 ILCS 5/11-130]

Section 11-134 also contains minimum-annuity formulas for employees with at least 20 years of service. One available formula uses 2.40% for each year of service and the highest average annual salary for any 4 consecutive years within the last 10 years. An annuity beginning before age 60 is generally reduced by 0.25% for each month or fractional month that the annuity begins before age 60. The statute also contains exceptions tied to longer service periods. [40 ILCS 5/11-134]

The Code does not provide enough information here to determine your pension amount. It turns on your applicable salary history, the amounts credited to your annuity accounts, and which Article 11 provision applies to your circumstances. The salary period used in the calculation may also depend on whether the post-2011 provisions apply. Section 1-160 says that those provisions apply to people who first became members on or after January 1, 2011, subject to its exceptions. [40 ILCS 5/1-160]

Waiting until age 60 is another important comparison. Section 11-129 addresses withdrawal at age 60 or older but before age 65 and calculates the annuity at your age on the withdrawal date. [40 ILCS 5/11-129]

Your pension would generally receive 3% annual increases under Section 11-134.1, subject to that section’s timing rules and contribution requirement. [40 ILCS 5/11-134.1]

cases.name: A survivor question that uses none of the survivor vocabulary

turns.question: My wife is worried about what happens to her if something happens to me. What would she get?
turns.answer:
If you die while still working and before age 65, your wife may receive a monthly widow’s annuity. It is calculated as of your date of death from the credits for your age-and-service annuity, widow’s annuity, and applicable prior-service credits. The statute does not provide enough information here to calculate her dollar amount. [40 ILCS 5/11-139]

The payment is an annuity: equal monthly payments for life, unless an event covered by the Code ends it. [40 ILCS 5/11-124] I could not establish from the sections available here exactly when a widow’s annuity ends because the relevant termination provision, Section 11-148, was not available.

If you leave service after age 55 but before age 60, Section 11-141 applies if you have at least 10 years of service. With 20 or more years of service, it uses the total widow’s-annuity credits and applicable prior-service widow’s credits when the annuity is fixed. [40 ILCS 5/11-141] If you leave service at age 60 or later but before age 65, Section 11-140 applies and uses the widow’s-annuity and applicable prior-service credits as of withdrawal. [40 ILCS 5/11-140]

Eligible unmarried children may also receive $220.00 per month each while your wife survives, or $250.00 per month each when no surviving spouse exists, subject to the family limits in the statute. [40 ILCS 5/11-153; 40 ILCS 5/11-154]

Your wife may not qualify in circumstances listed in Section 11-147, including certain marriages after withdrawal or after age 65, or if you received a refund of your annuity contributions. [40 ILCS 5/11-147]

turns.question: Does any of this get taxed, and do I still get health insurance?
turns.answer:
Your pension payments would generally be subject to federal income tax, but the Pension Code sections reviewed here do not establish the taxable portion or your withholding. The Code text does not answer that tax question.

Your Illinois state tax treatment also cannot be established from the Pension Code sections reviewed here.

Article 11 does not guarantee continuing retiree health insurance. It allows the retirement board, by regulation, to let an annuitant assign part of an annuity or disability benefit to pay premiums for hospital or medical insurance. The board may end that assignment right. [40 ILCS 5/11-223.1] The Code also allows certain payments to City annuitants who participate in City health plans, and to eligible Board of Education annuitants who choose a Board of Education retiree plan, but the payment periods stated in those sections ended on December 31, 2016. [40 ILCS 5/11-160.1] [40 ILCS 5/11-160.2]

So, the Code does not establish that you will keep health insurance after retirement. Your eligibility, coverage, premiums, and any current subsidy depend on the applicable retiree health plan and its rules.
